title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen (rikiyat.github.io)
comments:
Respectfully to the authors and to everyone here, I ask you to actually read the paper before losing your mind, or at the very least plug it into Claude. It is a cool project but not as nearly as insane as people say. I think the blog writing and subsequent posting overstate the results.Part of my research is in weight space learning. For starters, we have had the ability to edit weights, to generate new weights, to identify weights for a while. Here is an example for larger models as early as 2023:
https://rome.baulab.info/Weight space interpretability and learning is an active research community, has been for the past 3 years with many great papers. I suspect it is hitting non-interp folks harder because the authors hyped up their work, and people who are not in the field did not bother to read it before typing up X posts.Some experiments here are done on very small models (20K params). We already know that small models are more interpretable. In fact, much of editing here you can do by hand. For Qwen, the model fixed a looping bug that may have been known apriori, and it is basically a steering vector, a very established technique. This is clear when they then attempt to "improve" math capability, and it doesn't work. For me, this paper rather shows that OpenAI has done training on mechinterp  environment, in fact, maybe even on weight space learning datasets, which are open. But it does not show some insane "well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms" (from the blog post), more like past what I would expect from a large model with no specialized harness. I still think it is cool work, but do check out recent advances in autointerp, to ground your expectation.On a personal note, I understand the need for promotion of your work, but I think healthy skepticism is fine too. Otherwise, your understanding of what problems need to be worked on and solved in science becomes warped.reply

I think a lot of the upvotes, including mine, are just realizing that this is a thing. We can see implications of this as the model sizes scale up, just like early LLMs weren't as impressive, but we could see where they were heading.reply

Scale is an interesting point here. Large overparametrized networks don't behave in the same way as small toy models do; this is one of the big caveats of many interp works. I expect naked weight edit will not work for large models. Why? Because an agent needs to know what it edits and reason on it. You could theoretically improve a model on some form of weight recognition; maybe it will work, maybe it won't. But again, we come up against a cost/benefit dilemma; it sounds exotic and sci-fi but likely impractical. Parameters of the model are connected and relate to each other. Instead, current SOTA auto-interp argues that what we need are better tools for models to know themselves, so rather than direct edit, we need to give models better understanding of large parameter geometries, then they apply edits with non-destructive approaches at scale. This is much harder to do than applying a steering vector.reply

What I have been reading makes me want to both agree and disagree with your take here. I think the fact that some of these things are not only established but are much simpler than one would think at first glance yields the much cooler realization that you can not only do a lot more than abliteration, but that humans can do it by hand if the thing is made legible.From my experience with models when it comes to discernment about particular things, the models, even the best ones, still are not very good. The thing that we are most missing I think is acceleration in creating editing tools for humans that make the otherwise inscrutable both visually legible and interactive.reply
A sibling comment mentioned that self-editing weights is potentially a path to a self-improving system. Does that resonate with you?reply

It does, one of my ongoing research papers is about it. But I would ask people to take a look at the established idea of Hypernetworks: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.06955v3
Modern version of the field comes from Google Brain around 2016 https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.09106.In general my personal research thesis is that current deep learning is much less malleable and neuroplastic as it should be, I got into interpretability because of this. Many focus on safety, but I prioritize it as a toolbox that allows for greater shaping of the underlying intelligence system. If we can fully understand how learning happens, where information is stored and how it is processed, unlike in biological brains, we can apply edits and transformations in digital ones. And if I can use a technique to edit weights based on some underlying reasoning about a system (with a caveat that it leads to something worthwhile), so can an agent. Hence self-improvement. There are many interesting implication to weight space research, and I very much encourage people to read about it. But it is also very easy to overstate what is currently possible, in fact I'd say better to know what is not so one can make it possible.reply
Thank you for the perspective and context! Good grounding for understanding the topic.reply

> For Qwen, the model fixed a looping bug that may have been known aprioriIt was included in the prompt itself. The authors say they used claude code for the experiment, and claude wrote the prompt for astra, which included details of the looping bug. Then astra seems to have done h(looping) - h(loop fixed) and then gotten the usual steering vector.reply
Thank you for being the voice of moderation here. Good to hear a counterpoint from an authority on the topic.reply

Thanks, it's great to have some context. I think the most exciting thing about it is probably introducing a lot of people to a readily available low cost technique they can use to potentially build tiny models from scratch and/or tune an existing open weight model behaviorally. Yeah, nothing stunning is going to come out of it because you cannot unlock new capability, but even just being able to tweak the language of a model, make it slightly less sycophantic, boost a small model's ability to handle a case of interest slightly, I think changes the economics quite a bit, potentially. A world in which you use frontier models for the limited use case of tuning tinier more targeted ones is looking a lot more viable.reply
first_paragraph: Rikiya Takehi*Jayden Teoh*Alex ZhangOmar Khattab MIT CSAILMIT CSAILMIT CSAILMIT CSAILNovember 2, 2026We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. title: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise
comments: Just preordered -- glasses request: there's no way to say it nicely, I have a big nose. With a high bridge. Many glasses are really tough to get properly placed; may I request you not give up on the pads w/metal adjusters that you have in the product photos? Don't let a designer take them away from you, us folks not one standard deviation from 'normal' noses will thank you.Second, how tough is this signal processing? Will it be done on-glasses, or through an app? Third, what's the equivalent of a wake word for these? I'm reminded of the Apple Vision Pro radar to see if your fingers are clicking. I could imagine a lot of modalities where I want to just start talking and have things happen, and a lot where I don't want the glasses to pick it up. Fourth, I think a cool voice change demo would be rad -- not sure what latency is like, but if you could get it end to end under like 250ms you could probably have someone exaggerate the mouth movements and pipe out audio of them talking like someone else. Which would be another really cool demo.Super cool. You're going to be working 80 hour weeks for the next year, I'm excited to see what you put out!reply

Yep, we have been quite set on nose pads to keep them comfortable. I will keep you updated with the designs!The decoding is done via a companion app on your laptop or phone in the cloud, but end to end latency is still quite fast, under 500ms usually.To begin with we don't plan to have a wake word, but rather a trigger key on your connected device that you're entering text into (pressing Alt for example), similar to Wispr Flow. We're doing some R&D into the silent speech equivalent of voice activity detection, so we have a low power basic RF detection always-on, not enough to decode speech from but enough to detect rough movement, and when it detects speech-like activity beginning to start we can trigger full sensing within tens of ms. This would likely ship as a software update a few months after shipping, though.The voice change demo is something I've thought about actually, but we never got around to doing. Might film it soon :)reply

Also I note from your comments here you don’t plan on local inference - that seems like a huge self own, provided the model is less than like 2b params. I’m not saying people won’t in practice prefer your cloud version, but you have this huge uphill battle ahead of you on privacy which can be wiped at the stroke of a pen with “yep it will run on your Mac.”You can get both markets (ease of use and technical) by allowing it. Also i would bet that you gain almost no product security locking off local inference - the hardware is the hard bit. Once someone has your hardware in hand it will not take them long to reverse and build their own processing layer; you’ll need to fight those people on patents and product quality.Heck for a v1 just allowing local sensor data would probably be enough for the tech enthusiasts. But please don’t lock this off from the get go - it makes the sale harder and I don’t think it gives you much in return.reply

Agreed.Cloud processing can be tempting as the primary revenue stream, but it entirely cuts off those users who cannot send arbitrary PII over the internet (regardless of encryption promises).It also invites the (especially now-LLM-empowered) enthusiasts to reverse engineer it.Instead, consider selling the glasses with >20% profit, and give local users a cheaper subscription to something else (maybe the model updates?) so they can also help keep the company sustainable.reply

Super cool. For a cool voice change demo we'll allow a gb200 over low latency wifi :) elevenlabs has deals with a number of professional actors and voice actors for licensed uses, seems like you could probably find an ethical and cool co-brand opportunity in there.Have fun building this! It's worth doing.reply

> The decoding is done via a companion app on your laptop or phone in the cloud, but end to end latency is still quite fast, under 500ms usually.Why don't you do this on the phone? You don't want to have your proprietary tech on the user device? Or maybe you wanted to save the recording on your cloud anyway so you can train on it later or otherwise use the data?reply

Wait. You are taking the RF response, sending it up to the cloud to interpret, and then sending the result back? Hard pass from me, sorry. Cool tech, but I don’t want my internal thoughts anywhere near the cloud. Also, this would mean I couldn’t use something like this on the subway when the phone signal goes out intermittently, right?reply

The commercial reality I’m sure they’re dealing with is that the percentage of users who care enough to deal with everything required for local inference is nowhere close to large enough to make it into an initial launch.reply

Fair enough! We take data security and privacy very seriously and have built many safeguards to prevent even us from accessing the raw data in the cloud. At some point in the future we hope to launch local inference models too!reply

Respectfully, talk is cheap. Every company says they take security and privacy seriously even after their database has been breached and their customers' plaintext passwords and credit card details have become public information.If you were actually serious about prioritizing privacy above securing an ongoing service relationship you would ship local inference as the default and only (possibly later) offer a cloud service as an optional add-on for those who want/need it.reply

European RISC-V Industrial Computing Initiative
          RVA23 silicon has arrived. The industrial computer built on it has not.
          ERICI coordinates a reference stack, from firmware to real-time and
          general-purpose operating systems: it fixes the interfaces between the layers
          and verifies that they boot together on real RVA23 hardware. A box that boots
          it is ERICI-compatible.
        Why now
        Today's industrial computers run on x86 and Arm: two instruction sets, each
        owned and licensed by a single company. RISC-V is open, governed by a
